input_references.role: Compact timestamped trajectory points linked by trajectory_id

metadata.goal: Analyze differences in trajectory dynamics, speed change, and trip structure across trip purposes in the supplied multiple-user trajectories.
metadata.category: Purpose-conditioned trajectory dynamics, point-wise speed variation, and trip structure
metadata.header: MTL Trajet: 03 Purpose Time Distance Speed
metadata.dataset_description: MTL Trajet 2016 mobility data with trip purpose, mode, timing, endpoints, trip metrics, and Montréal PUM 2050 destination land-use categories. User IDs distinguish participants, and the point tables provide speed profiles. The single-user case includes a repeated work corridor.
metadata.metric_note: `longest_stable_run_points` is the longest consecutive GPS-point segment whose adjacent speed changes stay within the mode-specific limit recorded in `stable_speed_change_threshold_kmh`: walking 0.15, cycling 0.25, public transit 0.40, and motor vehicle 0.60 km/h. This local continuity metric is distinct from full-trajectory `point_speed_std_kmh`.
metadata.source_note: Historical trajectories (2016) are spatially matched to the 2025 official PUM land-use taxonomy; do not interpret the categories as historical 2016 land-use observations.

insight_list.question: Within each transport mode, how do comparable long work, shopping, and leisure trips differ in speed variability and continuous stable segments?

insights: Work- and education-related trajectories have more stable point-wise speed profiles, whereas shopping, dining, and leisure trajectories more often contain marked decelerations, stop/restart events, and renewed acceleration.

Shopping and dining trajectories entering Mixte destinations begin a sustained low-speed approach earlier in their progress, whereas work trajectories typically decelerate only closer to the destination.

Within both motor-vehicle and public-transit subsets of comparable longer-distance trajectories, work trips have longer continuous stable segments, while shopping or leisure trips show greater point-wise speed variability.
summary: Work and education trajectories have comparatively stable speed profiles, whereas shopping, dining, and leisure trajectories more often include deceleration and stop/restart behaviour. Shopping and dining trips begin sustained low-speed approaches to Mixte destinations earlier; within comparable longer motor-vehicle and public-transit trips, work retains longer continuous stable segments than shopping or leisure.
evidence_policy: Claims describe patterns in this dataset and do not establish causal relationships.
